- [ ] File is at `skills/<category>/<name>/SKILL.md` (not in `~/.hermes/skills/`) - [ ] Frontmatter starts at byte 0 with `---`, closes with `\n---\n` - [ ] `name`, `description`, `version`, `author`, `license`, `metadata.hermes.{tags, related_skills}` all present - [ ] Name ≤ 64 chars, lowercase + hyphens - [ ] Description ≤ 1024 chars, trigger phrase self-contained within first 57 chars, and starts with "Use when ..." - [ ] Total file ≤ 100,000 chars (aim for 8-15k) - [ ] Structure: `# Title` → `## Overview` → `## When to Use` → body → `## Common Pitfalls` → `## Verification Checklist` - [ ] Each ordered step has a checkable completion criterion - [ ] Description is trigger-focused and avoids duplicated body content - [ ] Bulky or branch-specific reference is progressively disclosed in linked files - [ ] No-op prose and duplicated rules removed - [ ] `related_skills` references resolve in-repo (or are explicitly OK to be user-local) - [ ] `git add skills/<category>/<name>/ && git commit` completed on the intended branch

skill.name: hermes-multi-agent-collaboration
skill.description: Coordinate multiple Hermes profiles on shared projects.
skill.skill_text:
--- name: hermes-multi-agent-collaboration description: Coordinate multiple Hermes profiles on shared projects. ---
# Hermes Multi-Agent Collaboration
Class-level knowledge for running several Hermes profiles (e.g. default + coder + testprofile) on the same coding projects without stepping on each other. All claims verified against the hermes source tree (hermes_constants.py, hermes_cli/main.py, hermes_cli/kanban_db.py, plugins/memory/*) on this machine.
## Session isolation (verified)
- Each profile has its OWN state.db at `<profile home>/state.db` (HERMES_HOME resolves per active profile). Session IDs live in that per-profile DB — they are NOT shared across profiles. - `hermes --resume <id>` / `--continue` only resolves sessions inside the ACTIVE profile's DB (main.py `_resolve_session_by_name_or_id` / `_resolve_last_session`). You cannot resume another profile's session by ID. - `--pass-session-id` injects the CURRENT session id into the system prompt (self-reference) — same profile only, NOT a sharing mechanism. - Cross-profile session access is READ-ONLY: session_search with a profile param, or `@session:<profile>/<id>` links. Read coder's history, never continue it.
## Kanban = the cross-profile task layer (verified)
- `~/.hermes/kanban.db` — durable SQLite board shared across ALL profiles. Tasks are claimed atomically; no two agents grab the same task. - One board per project/workstream: `hermes kanban boards create <slug>`. Each board has its own DB, workspaces directory, and dispatcher loop — tasks on one board cannot collide with tasks on another. Maps 1:1 to Bonfire project rooms by slug. - Create: `hermes kanban create TITLE [--assignee PROFILE] [--parent ID] [--project SLUG] [--workspace scratch|worktree|dir:...] [--max-runtime 30m] [--priority N] [--body "..."]`. Parents/children + runtime caps handle mixed task sizes; `--project` anchors the worktree under the project repo. - Dispatch runs the task in the ASSIGNED profile's HERMES_HOME (kanban_db.py propagates it) → the task's session lives in that profile's DB, with that profile's memory/skills. Tasks carry their own session_id column. - Auto-start is NOT the board's doing. The board is passive SQLite; a Ready task starts only when a dispatcher pass runs. Three dispatcher modes: (1) gateway-integrated loop (kanban.dispatch_in_gateway: true default — alive while the hermes gateway process runs), (2) standalone `hermes kanban daemon`, (3) manual one-shot sweep `hermes kanban dispatch [--dry-run]` (cron-able). CLI-only sessions with no gateway/daemon/cron → nothing auto-starts; a profile can still `hermes kanban claim` a Ready task by hand. - A dispatched worker is a FRESH session spawned under the assignee profile's home — the profile does NOT need an open chat. Workers get the focused kanban_* toolset (kanban_show/complete/block/heartbeat/comment/create/link) gated by env HERMES_KANBAN_TASK, board pinned via HERMES_KANBAN_BOARD. - Dispatch cadence: the embedded dispatcher ticks every `kanban.dispatch_interval_seconds` (default **60s**, floor 1.0s, junk → 60 + warning; THIS INSTALL IS SET TO **10s** as of 2026-09-16, set in `~/.hermes/config.yaml` and applied by a gateway restart). That setting is **machine-global, not per-profile**: the singleton lock is `kanban_home()/kanban/.dispatcher.lock` and `kanban_home()` resolves through `get_default_hermes_root()`, which returns the ROOT even when `HERMES_HOME` is a profile dir — so one dispatcher serves every profile and every board, and its interval comes from the config of the gateway that HOLDS the lock (here the default profile's `~/.hermes/config.yaml`; writing the key in a profile config is inert unless that gateway wins the boot race, and losers log "will NOT dispatch"). It is read ONCE at boot → tuning it needs `hermes gateway restart`, unlike toolset config. One tick sweeps all boards then sleeps the full interval, so N boards don't multiply latency. Don't quote 5s here — that's the separate notifier watcher. Detail, tuning risk (`max_spawn` / `max_in_progress`), and a read-only verification recipe: references/kanban-dispatch-cadence.md. Dispatcher auto-blocks a task after `kanban.failure_limit` consecutive spawn failures (default 2; per-task `max_retries` overrides). Kanban boards and Bonfire rooms are NOT wired together — posting in a Bonfire room never triggers the Hermes dispatcher (the slug mapping is a convention only). - Assignment IS the trigger (live-verified 2026-09 end-to-end): `hermes kanban assign <task_id> <profile>` from ANY profile session (plain CLI against the shared DB — no kanban_* toolset required) plus a live gateway flips the task ready→running within seconds. Claim event logs the lock as `<hostname>:<gateway-pid>`; the worker appears in ps as `hermes -p <profile> --cli ...` under the assignee's HERMES_HOME. Unassigned Ready tasks are never claimed — the dispatcher does not guess. Assigning starts real autonomous work (tokens, workspace, worker session in the assignee's DB), so treat the assign command as the launch trigger it is, not bookkeeping. - `kanban.orchestrator_profile` / `default_assignee` are OPTIONAL: used only by auto-decompose fan-out routing; when unset both fall back to the active default profile (hermes_cli/kanban_decompose.py `_resolve_orchestrator_profile`) so empty config never strands tasks. Dispatch itself needs only Ready + per-task assignee. - Workspace kinds: `scratch` is EPHEMERAL — deleted at task completion (the task logs a tip event warning about this). Use `--workspace worktree` or `--workspace dir:/abs/path` when worker output must survive completion. - Task memory = body + comments + `hermes kanban context <task_id>`; project memory = repo context files + the board. This IS the layered answer: task memory in kanban, project memory in the repo. - Worker end-of-task protocol (observed live): a dispatcher-spawned coding worker does NOT self-complete — it posts a handoff comment (design summary, verification results, open assumptions), attaches artifacts, then `kanban_block` with kind=needs_input, reason "review-required", and the run closes `blocked @coder`. Expect this shape: a task parked blocked/needs_input is a SUCCESSFUL delivery awaiting human approval, not a failure. To close: approve (complete) or send back for changes (comment + unblock → re-dispatch; the block event carries `recurrences`). - Quirk (observed): `kanban_attach` can silently truncate large base64 payloads on the first upload (saw a 738-byte stub for a ~30KB tarball). The worker self-corrected by overwriting the file, but the DB attachment metadata can keep showing the stale size — verify on-disk with stat/sha256sum, never trust the attachments listing alone. - Worker process signature: `hermes -p <profile> --cli --accept-hooks ...`, I/O-bound — sleeps (state Ssl) on the LLM API between tool calls at near-0% CPU; CPU only spikes during its terminal subprocess bursts (gem builds, tests). Near-idle parent CPU is the NORMAL healthy signature of a working agent, not a stalled worker.
## Project context files = shared project memory (verified)
- AGENTS.md (cwd only), .hermes.md (walks up to git root), CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules. First match wins; 20k char cap; loaded by ANY profile working in that cwd → cross-agent project memory with zero setup. - Any Hermes profile, Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode reading the same repo sees the same AGENTS.md. Put project rules/state there for all agents.
## Memory providers
- `hermes memory setup` offers: honcho, openviking, mem0, hindsight, holographic, retaindb, byterover (+ supermemory plugin dir). ONE external provider active at a time per profile; built-in MEMORY.md/USER.md always on. - Scoping is NOT native to any provider — you layer it. See references/memory-providers.md for the comparison table and the recommended 3-layer design (repo context files + kanban + one provider). - honcho is the only one with a directory→session mapping (`hermes honcho map <name>`), giving project-scoped sessions; both profiles can point at one honcho backend for genuinely shared memory. - OpenViking (ACTIVE provider on this machine, default profile) is source-verified shared-friendly: agent identity comes from env vars (OPENVIKING_ACCOUNT/USER/AGENT, defaults default/default/hermes) read per-profile from each profile's .env — NOT from the Hermes profile name. Enabling it in a second profile without overrides = same namespace = full shared memory; exact-path write mechanics and both sharing designs: references/openviking.md.
## Relaying between profiles (the manual bridge)
- One-shot: `hermes -p <profile> chat -q "<msg>"` (alias wrappers auto-created at ~/.local/bin/<name>, e.g. `coder`). - Persistent: tmux session running `hermes -p <profile>`, `tmux send-keys` to inject, `capture-pane` to read — keeps conversation context alive across relays. - Honest limit: no native cross-profile session sharing exists; relaying is a courier pattern (include conversation history in each query for context).
## Cross-profile delegation (options ladder)
- `delegate_task` is SAME-profile only: children are subagents in the parent profile (inherited profile home, model, memory, SOUL.md, skills, approvals mode, `.env` secrets, cwd) — never a route to coder/testprofile's isolated identity. Constraints verified in `tools/delegate_tool.py`: - Per-call knobs are ONLY `goal`, `context`, `role` (leaf|orchestrator), and toolset narrowing. There is NO per-child model or provider parameter in the tool schema. - Model pinning is PROFILE-level: `delegation.provider` / `delegation.model` apply to EVERY child. Empty = inherit the parent model and fallback chain. So one chat can fan out different JOBS and TOOLSETS per child, never different MODELS. - `delegation.max_spawn_depth` (this machine: 1) silently downgrades `role: orchestrator` to leaf — grandchildren are impossible. - Concurrency = `delegation.max_concurrent_children` (3 here), batch via `tasks=[...]`; each child capped by `delegation.max_iterations` (50). - Leaf children cannot call delegate_task, clarify, memory, send_message, or cronjob — a child can never ask the user a question mid-task. - Not durable: `/stop`, `/new`, or process exit discards running subagents. - Children share the parent's cwd (two children writing the same file WILL conflict) and see neither the parent conversation nor each other — pass context in, relay results out. - A child's final summary is a SELF-REPORT: verify external side effects (URL, file path, ID) yourself before claiming success. - Answer shape: in-profile fan-out ≠ different agents. Different identities/models/skills/memory require separate profiles (or the Bonfire/MCP layer). - Ladder, cheapest first: skill convention (codify the exact `hermes -p X chat -q` invocation) → one-shot `hermes -p <profile> chat -q "<full self-contained task>"` (synchronous; final reply returns in tool output) → tmux relay (persistent context) → native tool (plugin or MCP). - Turning the CLI invocation into a real tool is possible and verified: a directory plugin in ~/.hermes/plugins/<name>/ (plugin.yaml manifest + Python entry) can call PluginContext.register_tool(), which delegates to tools.registry.register() — the same registry built-in tools use. Full recipe, MCP variant, and pitfalls: references/cross-profile-delegation.md. - Spawned profiles know NOTHING of the parent conversation — pack all context (background, paths, acceptance criteria) into the single prompt; cross-profile context flows only through shared artifacts (files, kanban, AGENTS.md).
## Pitfalls
- Don't expect shared MEMORY.md across profiles — each profile has its own memories/ dir (default ~/.hermes/memories/ vs profiles/<name>/memories/). "Cross-profile memory" must be built from shared artifacts, never assumed. - Profile state (config, .env, skills, sessions, memory) is isolated by design; collaboration flows through state OUTSIDE the session: kanban board, repo context files, shared memory backend, Bonfire room messages. - When the user asks "can profile A see profile B's memory/session" the honest answer is: read-only session search at best; everything else needs the relay or shared-artifact pattern.

skill.name: hermes-observability
skill.description: Enable and verify Hermes tracing backends.
skill.skill_text:
--- name: hermes-observability description: "Enable and verify Hermes tracing backends." version: 1.0.0 author: Hermes Agent license: MIT platforms: [linux, macos, windows] metadata: hermes: tags: [hermes, observability, telemetry, tracing, langfuse, nemo-relay, plugins, hooks] category: autonomous-ai-agents related_skills: [hermes-agent, hermes-profile-admin] ---
# Hermes Observability (tracing / telemetry)
Covers tracing a Hermes instance with Langfuse, NeMo Relay, or any custom observer-hook consumer.
Hermes is **not traced by default**. It exposes a backend-neutral "observer hook" contract (`hermes.observer.v1`) and ships two opt-in observability plugins in the repo: `plugins/observability/langfuse/` and `plugins/observability/nemo_relay/`. Both are bundled but disabled until the user opts in. There is also a first-party NeMo Relay shared-metrics path that needs no plugin.
Hook contract + full field/correlation-ID reference: `references/observer-hooks.md`. Backend-specific enablement and install transcript: `references/langfuse-plugin.md`. Readiness probe: `scripts/check-langfuse.sh`.
## When to Use
- "Is Langfuse / tracing / telemetry enabled for this Hermes?" - "How do I trace this Hermes with Langfuse / NeMo Relay / an OTel collector?" - Enabling, verifying, or debugging a bundled observability plugin - Writing a custom observer plugin (hook names, fields, span correlation) - Any request to install a plugin's optional Python dependency into the Hermes venv (the uv-venv procedure below is generic)
## Answer the enablement question from the LIVE install — three checks
Never answer "enabled?" from memory or from the presence of config text. All three must hold; a "no" should say WHICH one is missing.
```bash # 1. plugin opt-in — authoritative hermes plugins list # Status column: enabled | not enabled # 2. SDK importable from the venv the agent actually runs "$HERMES_HOME/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python" -c "import langfuse; print(langfuse.__version__)" # 3. credentials — in .env, never config.yaml grep -i langfuse "$HERMES_HOME/.env" ```
Plugins load at agent startup, so even a fully-configured plugin exports nothing in a session that started earlier — a fresh session (`hermes chat -q "hello"`, or restart) is part of verification.
## Enable Flow (bundled Langfuse as the worked example)
- Interactive (does all three in one pass): `hermes tools` → **Langfuse Observability** → Cloud or Self-Hosted. The `post_setup` hook installs the SDK, writes the keys to `.env`, and adds the plugin to the enabled set. - Manual: install the SDK (below) → append keys to `.env` → `hermes plugins enable observability/langfuse` → `hermes plugins list` shows `enabled` → `hermes chat -q "hello"` → look for the "Hermes turn" trace in the backend.
Env vars: `HERMES_LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY`, `HERMES_LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY`, `HERMES_LANGFUSE_BASE_URL` (default `https://cloud.langfuse.com`; self-host is usually the UI port on :3000). Optional: `HERMES_LANGFUSE_ENV`, `HERMES_LANGFUSE_RELEASE`, `HERMES_LANGFUSE_SAMPLE_RATE`, `HERMES_LANGFUSE_MAX_CHARS` (default 12000/field), `HERMES_LANGFUSE_DEBUG=true`. NeMo Relay equivalent: `HERMES_NEMO_RELAY_*`.
## Installing a plugin's Python dependency into the Hermes venv (generic)
**The Hermes venv is created by `uv venv` and has NO pip** — `$HERMES_HOME/hermes-agent/venv/bin/pip` does not exist (its `bin/` holds `activate`, the `python` symlink, and console scripts, no pip). Any "install the SDK" instruction that shells out to `venv/bin/pip` fails with `no such file or directory`. Use uv, always `--dry-run` first:
```bash cd /tmp # see pitfall 2 — must be OUTSIDE the repo VIRTUAL_ENV="$HERMES_HOME/hermes-agent/venv" uv pip install --dry-run \ --python "$HERMES_HOME/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python" <package> # inspect the "+ new" / "~ upgraded" lines, then drop --dry-run ```
The dry run is not optional: it shows whether an already-pinned dependency in the agent's own venv (httpx, pydantic, aiohttp…) would be bumped. Confirm the result is additive, then re-check health with `hermes doctor`.
## Pitfalls
- **`[tool.uv] exclude-newer = "14 days"` blocks in-repo installs.** The repo's `pyproject.toml` sets a 14-day supply-chain cutoff plus an `exclude-newer-package` allowlist. Run uv **from inside `$HERMES_HOME/hermes-agent/`** and an index whose metadata omits upload dates fails with `No solution found when resolving dependencies` / "no versions of <pkg>" (uv even names a version it then refuses). `cd /tmp` first — outside a project, no cutoff applies. Or override per package: `--exclude-newer-package <pkg>=`. - **Index unreachable? Probe, don't guess.** `curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" https://pypi.org/simple/` — a timeout on the index while `files.pythonhosted.org` and general sites return 200 means the *index* is filtered/blocked, not the network. Test a few candidate mirrors, then pass `--index-url <working mirror>/simple`. Probe list and observed results: `references/langfuse-plugin.md`. - **Fail-open by design — silence is the default failure mode.** Missing SDK or missing/bad credentials make every hook no-op with no error and no warning. "No traces in the UI" is therefore NOT evidence of a crash; run the three checks and set `HERMES_LANGFUSE_DEBUG=true`. - **Langfuse key prefixes are validated** (`_LANGFUSE_KEY_PREFIXES`): public begins `pk-lf-`, secret begins `sk-lf-`. Placeholders like `test-key` are rejected at client construction and drop every trace. - **Secrets belong in `.env`; the enablement flag belongs to the plugin system.** Never hand-edit `config.yaml`, and never tell the user to put a non-credential setting in `.env`. - **Bundled ≠ third-party plugin path.** These plugins live in the repo's own `plugins/observability/<name>/` and `hermes plugins list` reports Source `bundled`. `hermes plugins enable observability/langfuse` is sufficient — do NOT tell the user to copy anything into `~/.hermes/plugins/`. (Per the repo contribution rubric, third-party observability backends ship as standalone plugin repos for exactly this reason.) - **Observer hooks are read-only telemetry.** Don't try to rewrite requests or results from them. The only behavior-affecting hooks are `pre_llm_call` (ephemeral context), `pre_tool_call` (can block), and `transform_tool_result` / `transform_llm_output` (replacements). Expensive payload construction is gated behind `has_hook(...)`, so instrumentation cost is only paid once a plugin registers the hook — preserve that if you write one.
## Verification
```bash bash scripts/check-langfuse.sh # or: bash scripts/check-langfuse.sh /path/to/HERMES_HOME ```
Prints the three readiness checks (enablement, SDK in venv, credential presence with prefix validation) plus a live import probe of the API surface the plugin needs (`Langfuse`, `propagate_attributes`, `start_as_current_observation`, `create_trace_id`, `flush`).
## Answer Shape
This user asks capability questions in short bursts and caps length. Lead with the verdict ("No — not enabled") then the two or three facts that change the decision, and cite the live evidence each claim came from (the `hermes plugins list` row, the `ModuleNotFoundError`, the empty `.env` grep) rather than paraphrasing docs. Hold the full enablement walkthrough behind an offer, and when an install is blocked by environment state, report the workaround you actually used — never hand the user a command you have not verified runs on this machine. If credentials are the only missing piece, say so plainly and ask for them (or for "self-hosted") instead of inventing keys.

skill.name: hermes-profile-admin
skill.description: Create, clone, configure, and verify Hermes profiles.
skill.skill_text:
--- name: hermes-profile-admin description: Create, clone, configure, and verify Hermes profiles. version: 1.0.0 author: Hermes Agent license: MIT platforms: [linux, macos, windows] metadata: hermes: tags: [hermes, profiles, configuration, multi-agent, cloning] category: autonomous-ai-agents related_skills: [hermes-agent] ---
# Hermes Profile Admin Skill
Create, clone, and configure isolated Hermes profiles (independent config, `.env`, SOUL.md personality, skills, sessions, and memory). This skill holds the profile-specific workflow and the gotchas that the bundled `hermes-agent` docs don't cover — load that skill for the full CLI reference, this one for the profile path.
Reference files: `references/providers-and-fallback.md` (per-profile model/provider/fallback), `references/context-files-vs-skills.md` (SOUL.md vs skill vs AGENTS.md loading semantics + the full per-profile isolation surface), `references/automation-surface.md` (cron per profile, hooks vs webhooks, `/plan` semantics), `references/mcp-vs-toolsets.md` (MCP is a separate axis from toolsets: per-profile `mcp_servers`, the `no_mcp` sentinel, deferred tool catalogs, the restart requirement), and `references/concurrency-and-scopes.md` (what is per-profile vs machine-global: delegation/cron/kanban caps, board-wide vs per-profile limits, and the kanban dispatch cadence), and `references/toolset-change-propagation.md` (does a tool toggle or MCP change need a gateway restart — the config→agent propagation path with source line numbers), `references/toolset-enumeration-surfaces.md` (the four surfaces that enumerate toolsets — 24/25/27/28 rows for the SAME profile — and which one a "how many toolsets do I have / which are active" request means). Starter SOUL copy: `templates/coder-soul.md`. Audit script: `scripts/profile-provider-audit.sh`. Bulk sync script: `scripts/sync-soul-profiles.sh` (one profile per SOUL.md in a source tree, with `.env` inheritance). Re-sync script: `scripts/soul-tree-resync.py` (source tree edited after the profiles exist — prints the per-profile delta, flags REMOVALS, backs up, mirrors). Cap report: `scripts/session-cap-report.py` (per-profile `max_concurrent_sessions` plus the live slot holders each profile's `runtime/active_sessions.json` records). Toolset census: `scripts/list-profile-toolsets.py` (per-profile `name,active` rows — offline via the real resolvers, or live via the dashboard API; `--csv` writes the file).
## When to Use
- "Create a profile named X" / "clone the default profile" - "Update the profiles from the SOUL folder" / "the SOUL.md files changed, sync them again" — source tree wins, but the delta (especially removals) must be reported first: see "Re-sync" + `scripts/soul-tree-resync.py` - Setting a per-profile personality (SOUL.md) or enabling tools/skills for one profile - Verifying a profile actually boots with its keys, personality, and tools - "How many toolsets do I have?" / "list my toolsets and whether they're active" / "make me a CSV of them" — the count depends on WHICH surface you count from (24, 25, 27 or 28 for one profile): `references/toolset-enumeration-surfaces.md` + `scripts/list-profile-toolsets.py` - "What differs between profiles?" / "Where does this rule go — SOUL.md or a skill?" - "Can one profile use several providers / fall back between them?" (see `references/providers-and-fallback.md`) - "Should this env var / API key / plugin be added to ALL profiles?" / "I changed the default `.env` — why doesn't profile X see it?" (per-profile snapshot semantics, see Pitfalls) - "Delete profile X" / "stop tracing profile X" — distinct requests, see Pitfalls before removing anything - "Explain cron / scheduled jobs for a profile", "is /hook messaging", "what is /plan" (see `references/automation-surface.md`) - "Does using MCP require the terminal tool?" / "which profiles can call MCP server X?" / "why aren't my MCP tools there?" (see `references/mcp-vs-toolsets.md`) - "Disable terminal / file / code execution on all profiles except X" (fleet-wide fail-closed lock-down — see "Fleet-Wide Toolset Lock-Down" below; do NOT just edit `platform_toolsets.cli`) - "I enabled/disabled a tool — do I need to restart the gateway?" / "my new tool isn't showing up" (no for toolsets — see "Does a Tool Toggle Need a Gateway Restart?" and `references/toolset-change-propagation.md`) - "Does a profile need the terminal/file toolset to read or write its skills?" / "are skills shared between profiles?" (no, and no — see `references/context-files-vs-skills.md`) - "Is that cap / interval per-profile or global?" — delegation, cron, kanban limits and the kanban dispatch cadence (see `references/concurrency-and-scopes.md`) - "Is there a max number of running sessions?" / "can I cap it globally?" / "why did a kanban worker die instantly?" — chat-session slots vs task caps: `max_concurrent_sessions` is per profile yet shared across that profile's CLI/TUI/dashboard/gateway surfaces, and only the messaging gateway needs a restart (see `references/concurrency-and-scopes.md`, plus `scripts/session-cap-report.py` for the live value + holders)
## Prerequisites
- `hermes` CLI on PATH (global flag `-p/--profile NAME` applies any subcommand to a profile: `hermes -p coder config show`) - Profiles live under `~/.hermes/profiles/<name>/` (or `$HERMES_HOME` when a profile is active)
## How to Run
```bash hermes profile create NAME --clone-from SOURCE --description "one-two sentence role description" ```
- `--clone` copies config.yaml, `.env`, SOUL.md, and skills from the ACTIVE profile. Prefer `--clone-from SOURCE` to name the source explicitly instead of depending on which profile is active. - `--description` feeds the kanban orchestrator's task routing (role, not just name). - An alias wrapper is auto-created at `~/.local/bin/<name>`; the new profile shows up in `hermes profile list` with a `◆` on the active one.
## Quick Reference
| Task | Command | |---|---| | Create/clone | `hermes profile create NAME --clone-from SOURCE --description "..."` | | List | `hermes profile list` | | Per-profile config | `hermes -p NAME config get/set KEY` | | Per-profile tools | `hermes -p NAME tools list --platform cli` / `tools enable TOOLSET --platform cli` | | Show details | `hermes profile show NAME` / `describe NAME` | | Smoke test | `hermes -p NAME chat -Q -q "..."` |
## Procedure
1. **Create**: `hermes profile create <name> --clone-from default --description "..."`. 2. **Personality**: write `<profile>/SOUL.md`. It is plain markdown injected as system-prompt identity slot #1 (`agent/prompt_builder.py::load_soul_md`). Cover identity, working style, communication rules, and boundaries (e.g. a coder profile: read-before-change, verify with real execution, no commits unless asked, no drive-by refactors). Starter copy: `templates/coder-soul.md`. 3. **Tools**: the clone inherits the source's `platform_toolsets.<platform>` lists. Add known toolsets with `hermes -p NAME tools enable X --platform cli`. Do NOT try to enable posture toolsets (see Pitfalls). 4. **Skills**: bundled skills are enabled by default; only `skills.disabled` / `skills.platform_disabled` turn them off. A clone inherits them all — "enabling" means confirming the relevant category exists under `<profile>/skills/` and nothing is disabled in its config. 5. **Verify** (below).
## Bulk Sync From a SOUL Directory (repo-driven profiles)
When a project keeps its agent identities as a tree of SOUL files (e.g. `<repo>/hermes/profiles/<group>/<soul-dir>/SOUL.md`) and wants one Hermes profile per soul, use `scripts/sync-soul-profiles.sh` instead of hand-running `hermes profile create` N times:
```bash bash scripts/sync-soul-profiles.sh /path/to/profiles \ [--clone-from default] [--dry-run] [--desc-file descriptions.tsv] [--skip NAME] ```
Layout it expects: `SOURCE/<group>/<soul-dir>/SOUL.md` (`SOUL.MD` accepted too; group depth arbitrary; `example` skipped by default). The soul-dir name becomes the profile id — lowercased, spaces → underscores, because the id must match `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]{0,63}` (so `normal message` → `normal_message`).
Per soul, idempotently: (1) `hermes profile create NAME --clone-from <clone-from>` if the profile is missing; (2) copy the SOUL to `<profile>/SOUL.md`, backing up the old one *only if it differs*; (3) copy the default profile's `.env` over (`chmod 600`) so keys are inherited; (4) set a role description via `hermes profile describe` **only when the profile has no `profile.yaml`**, so a curated description is never clobbered. Re-running is a no-op (`created=0`) — that is the acceptance test.
Then verify (see Verification below) — creation alone proves nothing about the `.env`, MCP, or skill inheritance of profiles that already existed.
### Re-sync: "update the profiles from the SOUL folder again"
The source tree is authoritative and the profile SOULs are mirrors, so a repeat request means: diff → report → mirror, never a blind overwrite. Run `python3 scripts/soul-tree-resync.py <SOURCE_TREE>` (dry-run first, `--apply` to write). What the run must produce, because the user reads the delta:
1. **Map by the file's own parent directory** — group dirs (`main/`, `bots/`) are not profiles; the leaf dir name is the id, lowercased, spaces → underscores (`main/normal message` → `normal_message`). `SOUL.MD` counts too. 2. **Print additions AND removals per profile.** Removal hunks are the ones that need eyes: they are either a deliberate edit by the user or a truncated save. List the removed lines (first few per hunk) verbatim in the reply so the user can catch the second case. Do NOT silently "restore" them. 3. **Back up the previous profile SOULs** to `<profiles>/.soul_backup_<YYYYmmdd_HHMMSS>/<profile>__SOUL.md` before writing (dot-prefixed, so the sweep never mistakes it for a profile — see Pitfalls), and keep the earlier backups around instead of overwriting them. 4. **Verify by re-reading bytes** (`open(src,'rb').read() == open(tgt,'rb').read()`) for all N targets, then run `hermes profile list` to prove the fleet still enumerates. `soul-tree-resync.py --apply` now does that re-read itself and prints `byte-verified after write: N/N targets`; a failed or non-identical write is reported as `WRITE-FAILED (<err>)` / `WRITE-MISMATCH` per profile, the batch still finishes, and the exit code goes 1 (it previously crashed on the first PermissionError and left the rest of the fleet unwritten with no report). SOUL.md is read per session, so no gateway restart is involved — say that explicitly rather than leaving the user to guess. 5. **Leave profiles with no source folder alone.** On this box that is `default` (`~/.hermes/SOUL.md`, which carries the Bonfire Collaboration Rules) and `testprofile`; the tree has no folder for either, so they are out of scope of "update all souls" and must be named as untouched in the reply.
In practice the tree moves in BOTH directions between rounds: round 1 the sources were strict SUPERSETS of the loaded files (additions only: the raw three-bullet memory list plus the appended `SECTION-xx` Bonfire page blocks — a straight byte copy was safe, and that was verified before writing); round 2 the sources had been edited to DELETE every `#### Related Profiles` cross-reference list (action 2, company 2, …, company_project 5 — 38 blocks total) and no additions; round 3 (2026-09-17) the sources gained per-role `#### W-bridge MCP Tools to Use` blocks under each SECTION-xx (additions only, +206 lines across 13 files — still a superset, so lossless); round 4 the same day added two NON-SECTION top-level policies to 12 of 13 files — `## Approval Request Tool Policy (2026-09-17)` (all 12; prefers `add_approve_request_with_message` over `add_approval_request`) and `## Workspace Bot Identity Policy (2026-09-17)` (the 7 execution-side profiles: action, company, company_project, cron_profile, knowledge, normal_message, not_known_task) — plus ONE tool-name swap in the three files that carried the old bullet. Same command both times, different verdict in the report. So check the direction of the diff every round instead of assuming "the source is newer therefore richer" — this is the difference between a safe copy and quietly dropping content the user still wanted.
Two things that make an edit round ambiguous, both seen in round 4, so surface them instead of deciding silently:
- **A file the user did NOT touch is a question, not a no-op.** `delegator` was byte-identical between source and mirror that round, which is exactly what a freshly-synced profile looks like — but it also means its source still carries `add_approval_request`, the tool-name the other 12 files just renamed away from. Report "X is unchanged / still has the old token" and let the user say whether it was deliberate; do NOT extend the policy to it on your own. - **The shared spec file can drift from the SOULs it feeds.** In this repo `hermes/shared/profile-knowledge-sections.md` is the documented origin of the appended `SECTION-xx` blocks, and that round it received the tool-name swap (line 48) but NOT the two new top-level policies, which exist only in the 12 SOULs. Mirroring the SOULs is the requested job; note the divergence in the reply (it affects the next regeneration) rather than editing the spec file.
## Fleet-Wide Toolset Lock-Down (`agent.disabled_toolsets`)
To remove a toolset (terminal, file, code_execution, …) from EVERY entry point of a profile, edit `agent.disabled_toolsets` — not the per-platform lists.
Why the per-platform route fails: `platform_toolsets` is an ALLOWLIST keyed by platform, and the platform that matters for bots is not `cli`. W-bridge/bot traffic calls the multiplexed API server (`/p/<profile>/v1/chat/completions`), and `gateway/platforms/api_server.py` resolves via `_get_platform_tools(config, "api_server")` — falling back to the `hermes-api-server` platform default when the key is absent (which it is in most fleets), and that default INCLUDES terminal/file/code_execution. So a profile can show a terminal-free `cli` list while still handing a bot a shell. Same class of hole: the `cron` platform key, and messaging-platform composites.
`agent.disabled_toolsets` is subtracted LAST inside `tools_config._get_platform_tools()` ("This runs last so it overrides everything above"), so one list covers cli, api_server, cron, every messaging platform, and delegated subagents (`tools/delegate_tool.py` inherits parent enabled/disabled). `cron/scheduler.py::_resolve_cron_enabled_toolsets` merges it into its disabled list too, so per-job `enabled_toolsets` can't re-enable it.
Procedure (no CLI can do this — the key is a list, and `hermes config set` writes scalars only):
```python import re, shutil, datetime block = " disabled_toolsets:\n - terminal\n - file\n - code_execution\n" p = f"/home/user/.hermes/profiles/{name}/config.yaml" t = open(p).read() assert not re.search(r"^\s*disabled_toolsets:", t, re.M) # idempotence shutil.copy2(p, p + ".bak-" + datetime.datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d-%H%M%S")) lines = t.split("\n") i = next(i for i, l in enumerate(lines) if l.startswith("agent:")) # top-level agent: lines[i+1:i+1] = block.rstrip("\n").split("\n") open(p, "w").write("\n".join(lines)) ```
Surgical insertion (not a YAML round-trip) is deliberate: configs carry comments a `yaml.dump` would erase. Back up first, insert right after the top-level `agent:` line, then verify.
Verify in two layers.
1. Offline, per profile — fresh process, `HERMES_HOME` set, so nothing is cached across profiles:
```python import os, sys; os.environ["HERMES_HOME"] = home sys.path.insert(0, "/home/user/.hermes/hermes-agent") from hermes_cli.config import load_config from hermes_cli.tools_config import _get_platform_tools cfg = load_config(); blocked = {"terminal", "file", "code_execution"} for plat in ["cli", "api_server", "cron", "telegram", "discord"]: leak = blocked.intersection(_get_platform_tools(cfg, plat)) print(plat, "LEAK:" + ",".join(sorted(leak)) if leak else "CLEAN") ```
2. Live, through the running gateway — proves it took effect without a restart (config reads are mtime-keyed, so no gateway restart is needed):
```bash K=$(python3 -c "import yaml;print(yaml.safe_load(open('$HOME/.hermes/config.yaml'))['API_SERVER_KEY'])") curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $K" http://127.0.0.1:8642/p/<profile>/v1/toolsets # -> {"platform":"api_server","data":[{"name":"terminal","enabled":false},...]} ```
The endpoint reads the profile's own config (HERMES_HOME override from the `/p/<profile>/` prefix) and reports `platform: "api_server"` — it is the same resolution the agent gets, minus MCP (called with `include_default_mcp_servers=False`, so a configured MCP server stays enabled even though it isn't listed).
Caveats: - **Entries must be exact toolset KEYS, not UI labels.** Users dictate from the Built-in Toolsets UI, which shows labels; map them before writing or the entry silently no-ops. Live mapping (this install): `Computer Use (macOS/Windows/Linux)`→`computer_use`, `Discord Server Admin`→`discord_admin`, `Discord (read/participate)`→`discord`, `Speech-to-Text`→`stt`, `BFL FLUX 3 Video`→`bfl`, `Text-to-Speech`→`tts`, `Image Generation`→`image_gen`, `Vision / Image Analysis`→`vision`, `Video Analysis`→`video`, `Video Generation`→`video_gen`. Doubt: enumerate `_get_effective_configurable_toolsets()` from `tools_config.py` and print `key | label`. Watch for near-neighbours — `video` vs `video_gen` are separate rows, so "disable the video ones" needs both named explicitly. - A profile with NO `config.yaml` (a bare `profiles/<name>/` with only `cron/`) cannot be locked down until one exists — `load_config()` then returns built-in defaults. Create a minimal `config.yaml` holding just `agent:` + `disabled_toolsets:`. Note such a profile also has no `API_SERVER_KEY`, so its `/p/<name>/v1/toolsets` route answers `Invalid gateway API key` and can only be verified offline (layer 1). - Importing `hermes_cli.*` while pointed at a bare profile creates empty `hooks/`, `pairing/`, `skills/` scaffolding dirs. `rmdir` them if you want the tree left exactly as found. - Reversing = delete the `disabled_toolsets` lines (keep the backup path in the report so the user can diff/restore). - **Lock-downs arrive in BATCHES — each batch is scoped to the items it names.** A follow-up "also disable A, B, C for all profiles" means apply A/B/C; it does NOT re-open the scope decision made for the previous batch. Failure mode to avoid: keeping one accumulated DENY list in the script and unioning it into every profile, which silently revokes an exemption the user granted earlier. This happened in-session — the accumulated 11-item list was written to the two profiles deliberately exempted from terminal/file, and had to be pulled back out mid-turn. Rules: drive each batch from that batch's own key list; decide per profile between "append to the existing block" and "leave untouched"; and print a per-profile `declared(...)` diff in the report so over-reach is visible in the very next command. Re-read the standing exemption list before every batch (here: `default` + `coder` keep terminal/file/code_execution). - **Appending to an existing block is a different edit from creating one.** Batch 1 inserts after the top-level `agent:` line; batch N must locate the existing `disabled_toolsets:` key, consume the following `- ` item lines, diff against the new keys, and splice. Verify by re-reading the declared list per profile, not by trusting the write. - `hermes profile list` / `hermes tools list` do NOT show this switch, so state it explicitly in the reply; a user re-enabling via the Desktop Toolsets UI will find the toggle "saves" but stays off (`tools_config.py` clears `agent.disabled_toolsets` only for toolsets the user re-enables for a platform).
## Does a Tool Toggle Need a Gateway Restart?
**No — not for a built-in toolset toggle.** Same answer for every platform key (`cli`, `telegram`, `api_server`, …): the gateway re-reads config per message and rebuilds its cached agent when the toolset set changes. Verified in source:
- `hermes tools enable/disable X` persists into `platform_toolsets.<platform>` (`hermes_cli/tools_config.py` ~L2527-2566) — no CLI writes lists, which is also why the fleet lock-down above is a hand edit. - Per message the gateway runs `_load_gateway_config()` (mtime-keyed raw-yaml cache → an edit on disk is visible immediately) then `enabled_toolsets = sorted(_get_platform_tools(user_config, platform_key))` (`gateway/run.py` ~L24038-24044; background-task path ~L19233-19251). - The cached AIAgent is keyed by `_agent_config_signature(...)`, whose blob includes `sorted(enabled_toolsets)`, plus `_CACHE_BUSTING_CONFIG_KEYS` — a tuple that explicitly lists `("agent", "disabled_toolsets")` (`gateway/run.py` ~L22225-22247, signature ~L22336-22402, commented as values "baked at construction" that would otherwise be silently ignored until some other eviction). A toolset edit therefore changes the signature, the cached agent is discarded and rebuilt on the NEXT message, and the new toolset is live. No gateway restart, no manual eviction.
Two boundaries, and they are part of the answer:
1. **Not instantaneous mid-conversation.** A running agent keeps its frozen toolset until the rebuild, which invalidates that session's prompt-cache prefix (deliberate trade, per the AGENTS.md cache invariant). If a toggle seems not to land, the fix is `/reset` (new session), never `/restart`. 2. **MCP servers are a different axis.** Adding/removing an *MCP server* is reconnected live by the gateway slash command `/reload-mcp` (`gateway/run.py::_execute_mcp_reload` ~L20086 — reports reconnected/added/ removed servers + available tool count). Still not a full restart.
What a **gateway restart** IS for: Hermes code/plugin changes, platform/channel wiring, and machine-global boot-read knobs (e.g. `kanban.dispatch_interval_seconds`). In-chat that is `/restart` (`gateway/slash_commands.py::_handle_restart_command` — drains active work, then restarts the process); from a shell, `hermes gateway restart`. On the **CLI** surface toolsets are baked into the running agent, so a CLI session needs a new session (`/reset`, `/new`) or a relaunch — the gateway-restart question does not apply there.
Source line numbers and verification probes: `references/toolset-change-propagation.md`.
## Pitfalls
- **Posture toolsets cannot be manually enabled.** `coding` is marked `"posture": True` in `toolsets.py`; `hermes tools enable coding` fails with `✗ Unknown toolset 'coding'`. It auto-activates per-session via `agent/coding_context.py` whenever the session is in a code workspace (default `agent.coding_context: auto`) and propagates to delegated subagents. Don't fight it — the posture is the feature. - **`hermes config set` writes scalars only.** `set_config_value` in `hermes_cli/config.py` coerces bool/int/float but never parses lists/JSON. You cannot set a list key like `platform_toolsets.cli` with it. Use `hermes tools enable/disable` for toolsets instead. - **The dashboard's Config page is a THIRD write path with the SAME comment hazard — and a type quirk.** `PUT /api/config` deep-merges the form into the raw file; the YAML toggle on that page (`PUT /api/config/raw`) parses the whole document and re-dumps it with `merge_existing=False`. Both go through the YAML dumper, so a comment-rich config comes back comment-free exactly like `hermes config set` (this box's root config would lose its 36 comments). Two more quirks when sending a user to the UI instead of the CLI: the form is generated from `DEFAULT_CONFIG`, so a field whose default is `null` (e.g. `max_concurrent_sessions`) infers a **string** type and renders as a plain text input that saves a quoted value (loaders coerce numeric strings, so it still works); and the field set is whatever the RUNNING version ships. Before naming a control to click, confirm it exists with `GET /api/config/schema` — that endpoint answers WITHOUT a token, while `GET/PUT /api/config` need one. - **The "⚠ This profile has no API keys yet" warning after a clone is generic.** `.env` (provider keys included) IS copied by `--clone`. Trust the smoke test, not the warning. - **Toolset taxonomy surprises**: `project` is GUI-sessions-only (Desktop), `debugging` is a scenario toolset that only bundles terminal/web/file (usually redundant when those are already enabled). - **Four surfaces enumerate toolsets, so a count is never "wrong" by itself — find the surface the user is counting.** For one profile this box answers 24 (`_checklist_toolset_keys`, the interactive checklist), 25 (`hermes -p NAME tools list --platform cli`, resolved built-ins only), 27 (`_get_effective_configurable_toolsets()`, the configurator universe incl. config-only `stt`), or 28 (`GET /api/tools/toolsets?profile=NAME` on the dashboard, which also carries plugin toolsets discovered in that process — `a2a` here). A user quoting a number is usually reading the dashboard: match it and name the surface yours came from instead of replying "there are only 25". Auth/port recipe + the `name,active` CSV shape: `references/toolset-enumeration-surfaces.md`, `scripts/list-profile-toolsets.py`. - **`hermes tools` refuses to run non-interactively — scripting must go around it.** Both `hermes tools` and `hermes tools --summary` exit with `Error: 'hermes tools' requires an interactive terminal. It cannot be run through a pipe or non-interactive subprocess.`; a pty does NOT bypass it. Use `hermes tools list --platform NAME` (prints `✓ enabled` / `✗ disabled` rows plus a separate "MCP servers" block — never count those lines as toolsets) or the dashboard API. Related doc drift: `cli-config.yaml.example` (~L1025) still advertises `hermes chat --list-toolsets`, which this build rejects as `unrecognized arguments`. - **Never hand-edit a profile's config.yaml** — use `hermes config set` / `hermes tools`; a stray indent breaks YAML loading. The one exception is `agent.disabled_toolsets` (and other list-valued keys): no CLI writes lists, so back the file up, insert the block after the top-level `agent:` line, and re-verify by loading the config (`load_config()` runs the YAML linter) — see "Fleet-Wide Toolset Lock-Down". - **`platform_toolsets.cli` is not the list bots get.** Each gateway surface has its own platform key (`api_server`, `cron`, `telegram`, …) and an absent key falls back to that platform's default toolset, so "I removed terminal from the profile" can be true of the CLI and false of bot/API traffic. Only `agent.disabled_toolsets` is cross-surface. See "Fleet-Wide Toolset Lock-Down". - **There is no `role` field on a profile.** `<profile>/profile.yaml` holds exactly `description` + `description_auto` (`hermes_cli/profiles.py`, `read_profile_meta` / `write_profile_meta`). The source comment only CALLS the description the profile's role — it is free prose the kanban decomposer reads for routing. No role list, no per-role settings, no role→model map; a profile with no `profile.yaml` routes by name alone. Set it with `hermes profile describe NAME --text "..."`, or `--auto` to draft it with `auxiliary.profile_describer` (marks `description_auto: true` → review badge). So "can one profile have multiple roles?" -> functionally yes (skills across domains + a multi-capability description + the 14 `auxiliary.*` slots each on its own provider), structurally no (no role container). Distinct identities/models/memory = distinct profiles. - **`hermes profile show` takes the NAME positionally.** `hermes -p coder profile show` fails with `the following arguments are required: profile_name` — that subcommand has its own positional arg and does not read the global `-p`. Use `hermes profile show coder`. `-p` does work on the config-reading subcommands (`config get/set`, `config env-path`, `tools`, `fallback`). - **SOUL.md is always injected; a skill is not.** A rule that must apply every time belongs in SOUL.md (a short imperative); procedure/tables/commands belong in a skill. SOUL.md cannot enable or disable tools — enforcement is `hermes tools`. Full decision matrix and the complete per-profile isolation surface: `references/context-files-vs-skills.md`. - **`/hook` does not exist, and hooks are not messaging.** There is no `/hook` command in `hermes_cli/commands.py`; `hooks:` in config.yaml are shell-script LIFECYCLE hooks (`hermes hooks list/test/doctor`), inbound/outbound webhooks are a separate HTTP trigger/delivery system, and messaging platform adapters are a third thing. Don't let a user's naming convention pull the answer into the wrong system — say plainly that the term doesn't exist as a command, then give the nearest real concept. Detail: `references/automation-surface.md`. - **`/plan` is a skill-backed one-turn mode, not a separate command.** It isn't in the slash-command registry — it works because `/<name>` loads a skill, and `plan` is a PROTECTED built-in (`tools/skill_usage.py`) the curator must never archive (archiving turns `/plan` into "Unknown command" silently). It is plan-only for that turn, writes to `.hermes/plans/`, and the execution half happens in the NEXT normal message, same session — no restart, no persistent mode to exit. Detail: `references/automation-surface.md`. - **Cron is per-profile and gateway-owned.** Each profile has its own job table; nothing fires while the gateway is stopped (`hermes cron status`). Jobs created from a CLI session are LOCAL-ONLY — output is saved and readable but there is no live delivery into a terminal, so notification requires `deliver` pointing at a gateway-connected platform. Never promise a `deliver='origin'` cron job will message the user in a CLI session. Detail: `references/automation-surface.md`.
- **`hermes mcp add` is interactive — and saves `enabled: false` when the server isn't up.** It prompts "Does this server require authentication? [Y/n]", then (after a failed connect) "Save config anyway? [y/N]", then "Enable all N tools? [Y/n/select]". Pipe the answers (`printf 'n\ny\n' | hermes -p NAME mcp add X --url ... --connect-timeout 10`); a pty is not required. If the endpoint isn't listening you get `✓ Saved 'X' to config (disabled)` — the entry lands with `enabled: false` + a `connect_timeout`, which does NOT match a sibling profile's bare-`url` entry. Remove those two keys with a targeted `patch` (YAML re-checked by the linter) so the server is enabled like its peers, and confirm with `hermes -p NAME mcp list` showing `✓ enabled`. - **MCP does NOT require the terminal tool — do not answer otherwise.** `mcp_servers` is a top-level, per-profile config key on its own axis; each enabled server becomes a runtime toolset named after itself and is folded into the enabled set by `tools_config.py`. Proven live: the `delegator` profile has terminal removed from `platform_toolsets.cli` and still loads `w-bridge` + `memory`. stdio servers are spawned by `tools/mcp_tool.py`'s own asyncio subprocess path, never through the model-facing terminal tool. The only opt-out is the `no_mcp` sentinel. Two follow-ons worth stating up front: MCP discovery happens at agent STARTUP, so a server added mid-session is invisible to the running agent — in a gateway `/reload-mcp` reconnects servers live (see "Does a Tool Toggle Need a Gateway Restart?"), on the CLI only a new session is; and a large server's tools may arrive via the deferred `tool_search`/`tool_call` catalog instead of the system-prompt index. Detail + fleet audit snippet: `references/mcp-vs-toolsets.md`. - **A clone only carries config/.env/skills into a *new* profile; an already-existing profile keeps its own.** So after a bulk sync, diff the pre-existing profiles against the source: `hermes -p NAME mcp list`, and compare skill trees (`diff <(cd $HERMES_HOME/skills && find . -name SKILL.md | sort) <(cd profiles/NAME/skills && find . -name SKILL.md | sort)`). A profile can look fine (right SOUL) while being unable to call the tools that SOUL tells it to use. - **Writing a SOUL is not "updating a profile".** The SOUL is identity text only — it cannot enable MCP servers, toolsets, or skills. When a soul references specific tools (`add_loading_message`, `project_todos*`), treat the tool wiring as a separate, explicit deliverable. - **`.env` inheritance is a one-time SNAPSHOT, not a live link.** A profile reads its own `<profile>/.env` (`hermes_cli/config.py::get_env_path()` → `get_hermes_home() / ".env"`). `profiles.py::backfill_profile_envs()` copied the default `.env` into each named profile exactly ONCE, at the migration that made credentials profile-scoped, and never re-syncs ("Users can then diverge per profile from there"); `--clone` and `sync-soul-profiles.sh` likewise COPY at create/run time. So a key added to the default `.env` afterwards exists in NO profile — verified live: root had 3 `HERMES_LANGFUSE_*` keys, all 14 profiles had 0. Same trap for plugin opt-in: `plugins.enabled` is written by `plugins_cmd._save_enabled_set()` → `save_config()`, i.e. into the ACTIVE profile's `config.yaml`. To change something fleet-wide, loop the CLI (`hermes -p NAME config set KEY VAL`, `hermes -p NAME plugins enable X`); for env-var sweeps use `hermes-observability/scripts/rollout_langfuse_to_profiles.py` (idempotent, `--remove` to undo). Always verify per profile afterwards — `hermes -p NAME config get KEY`, `hermes -p NAME plugins list`. - **A SOUL source tree is not guaranteed to be a SUPERSET of the profile files.** "Update the profiles from the SOUL folder" can mean additions, deletions, or both, and the source can shrink between rounds (observed: round 1 additions only, round 2 a deliberate deletion of all `#### Related Profiles` blocks). Always diff first and list the removals in the reply; mirror the tree as asked (source wins), but never assume a straight copy is lossless — see "Re-sync: 'update the profiles from the SOUL folder again'" and `scripts/soul-tree-resync.py`. Also: profiles with no matching source folder (`default`, `testprofile` on this box) are out of scope and stay untouched. - **Never hand-roll the re-sync as an inline `cp` loop — the backups collide.** Every source file is named `SOUL.md`, so `cp -p "$tgt/SOUL.md" "$BACKUP/"` into ONE flat backup dir overwrites the same path 13 times; you keep the last profile's file and silently lose the other 12 snapshots (observed live, round 3 of this tree). Two fixes, both already in the scripts: back up as `<BACKUP>/<profile>__SOUL.md` (flat, unique names — what `soul-tree-resync.py` and `sync-soul-profiles.sh` write), or `<BACKUP>/<profile>/SOUL.md` (per-profile subdir, what `sync-soul-profiles.sh` writes). The inline-loop route also blows the 50-call sandbox cap on 13 profiles when each copy is verified separately — run one script file instead of per-file tool calls. Recovery when it has already happened: if the source tree is a strict superset (additions only), nothing is lost — the pre-sync mirror was byte-identical to the previous source revision, so rebuild the backup with `git show HEAD~1:<path-to-SOUL.md>` and confirm one survivor with `cmp` before trusting it. - **Re-sync acceptance test = run `scripts/soul-tree-resync.py <SRC>` dry-run and read `changed: 0`.** That is the cheapest proof the mirror is complete; it also prints `removed lines:` so a deletion round can't pass unnoticed. Follow with `hermes profile list` (fleet still enumerates) and state that SOUL.md is read per session so no gateway restart is involved. - **Not every directory under `profiles/` is a profile.** Backups such as `.soul_backup_20260914_095345` sit in the same tree; treat a directory as a profile only when it has `config.yaml`, or a `for d in profiles/*/` sweep writes credentials into backups. - **`hermes profile delete NAME -y` removes the directory AND the CLI alias.** Output: `✓ Removed ~/.local/bin/NAME` then `✓ Removed ~/.hermes/profiles/NAME`, after listing what goes (config, API keys, memories, sessions, skills, cron jobs). Before running it: (a) archive first if there is any chance the user wants something back — `tar czf /tmp/NAME-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S).tar.gz -C ~/.hermes/profiles NAME` (a test profile of ~18M compresses to ~5M); (b) unwind anything you attached to that profile (per-profile credentials, plugin opt-ins) so it does not outlive the directory; (c) say plainly that telemetry already exported to an external backend is NOT deleted with the profile. `-y` is the only guard, so treat the alias removal as the point of no return for `NAME`-as-a-command. If the request is ambiguous between "delete the profile" and "stop tracing it", ask — the two differ by irreversible data loss.
## Answer Shape
This user asks capability questions in short bursts and explicitly caps length ("answer short"). Lead with the verdict plus the one or two facts that change the decision, and hold the exhaustive detail behind an offer to go deeper. Settle what can be settled by reading the live install — `hermes -p NAME config get`, `hermes <cmd> --help`, the source tree at `~/.hermes/hermes-agent/` — and name the file or command the answer came from instead of reciting docs. When the user's term is not a real field or command ("role", "/hook"), say so first, then give the nearest real concept.
**Fleet-wide requests: ask which SET, then answer the scope question as the deliverable.** "Disable X for all profiles" is ambiguous in a way that matters, because `default` is the user's own interactive profile. Ask once, with concrete choices (all N / bots only / all except default), and lead the reply with the set you touched. Observed split on this box: the user exempts `default` + `coder` from capability-stripping toolsets (terminal/file/code_execution) but answers "literal all profiles" for peripheral ones (vision, image_gen, tts, stt, discord, computer_use, bfl). Never guess silently — but never ask twice about the same batch either, and don't widen a later batch to re-litigate an earlier decision.
Also: when a config question's answer is a scope (per-profile vs global), state the scope as the verdict, then the proof — the live value, the file/line it came from, and whether applying a change needs a restart. That structure is what this user reads for. Restart-or-not questions follow the same shape: verdict with the negation spelled out ("No — not for a tool toggle"), then the one-line mechanism and the source it came from, then the boundary cases that DO need a restart — work from `references/toolset-change-propagation.md`.
## Verification
```bash hermes -p NAME chat -Q -q "State your identity in one sentence, then reply with exactly: PROFILE-OK" ```
Expect the SOUL.md identity text in the reply plus the marker. A correct reply proves config, `.env` keys, model, and personality all load end-to-end.

skill.name: himalaya
skill.description: Himalaya CLI: IMAP/SMTP email from terminal.
skill.skill_text:
--- name: himalaya description: "Himalaya CLI: IMAP/SMTP email from terminal." version: 1.1.0 author: community license: MIT platforms: [linux, macos, windows] metadata: hermes: tags: [Email, IMAP, SMTP, CLI, Communication] homepage: https://github.com/pimalaya/himalaya prerequisites: commands: [himalaya] ---
# Himalaya Email CLI
Himalaya is a CLI email client that lets you manage emails from the terminal using IMAP, SMTP, Notmuch, or Sendmail backends.
This skill is separate from the Hermes Email gateway adapter. The gateway adapter lets people email the agent and uses Hermes' built-in IMAP/SMTP adapter; this skill lets the agent operate a mailbox from terminal tools and requires the external `himalaya` CLI.
## References
- `references/configuration.md` (config file setup + IMAP/SMTP authentication) - `references/message-composition.md` (MML syntax for composing emails)
## Prerequisites
1. Himalaya CLI installed (`himalaya --version` to verify) 2. A configuration file at `~/.config/himalaya/config.toml` 3. IMAP/SMTP credentials configured (password stored securely)
### Installation
```bash # Pre-built binary (Linux/macOS — recommended) curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pimalaya/himalaya/master/install.sh | PREFIX=~/.local sh
# macOS via Homebrew brew install himalaya
# Or via cargo (any platform with Rust) cargo install himalaya --locked ```
## Configuration Setup
Run the interactive wizard to set up an account:
```bash himalaya account configure ```
Or create `~/.config/himalaya/config.toml` manually:
```toml [accounts.personal] email = "you@example.com" display-name = "Your Name" default = true
backend.type = "imap" backend.host = "imap.example.com" backend.port = 993 backend.encryption.type = "tls" backend.login = "you@example.com" backend.auth.type = "password" backend.auth.cmd = "pass show email/imap" # or use keyring
message.send.backend.type = "smtp" message.send.backend.host = "smtp.example.com" message.send.backend.port = 587 message.send.backend.encryption.type = "start-tls" message.send.backend.login = "you@example.com" message.send.backend.auth.type = "password" message.send.backend.auth.cmd = "pass show email/smtp"
# Folder aliases (himalaya v1.2.0+ syntax). Required whenever the # server's folder names don't match himalaya's canonical names # (inbox/sent/drafts/trash). Gmail is the common case — see # `references/configuration.md` for the `[Gmail]/Sent Mail` mapping. folder.aliases.inbox = "INBOX" folder.aliases.sent = "Sent" folder.aliases.drafts = "Drafts" folder.aliases.trash = "Trash" ```
> **Heads up on the alias syntax.** Pre-v1.2.0 docs used a > `[accounts.NAME.folder.alias]` sub-section (singular `alias`). > v1.2.0 silently ignores that form — TOML parses fine, but the > alias resolver never reads it, so every lookup falls through to > the canonical name. On Gmail this means save-to-Sent fails *after* > SMTP delivery succeeds, and `himalaya message send` exits non-zero. > Any caller (agent, script, user) that retries on that exit code > will re-run the entire send — including SMTP — producing duplicate > emails to recipients. Always use `folder.aliases.X` (plural, dotted > keys, directly under `[accounts.NAME]`).
## Hermes Integration Notes
- **Reading, listing, searching, moving, deleting** all work directly through the terminal tool - **Composing/replying/forwarding** — piped input (`cat << EOF | himalaya template send`) is recommended for reliability. Interactive `$EDITOR` mode works with `pty=true` + background + process tool, but requires knowing the editor and its commands - Use `--output json` for structured output that's easier to parse programmatically - The `himalaya account configure` wizard requires interactive input — use PTY mode: `terminal(command="himalaya account configure", pty=true)`
## Common Operations
### List Folders
```bash himalaya folder list ```
### List Emails
List emails in INBOX (default):
```bash himalaya envelope list ```
List emails in a specific folder:
```bash himalaya envelope list --folder "Sent" ```
List with pagination:
```bash himalaya envelope list --page 1 --page-size 20 ```
### Search Emails
```bash himalaya envelope list from john@example.com subject meeting ```
### Read an Email
Read email by ID (shows plain text):
```bash himalaya message read 42 ```
Export raw MIME:
```bash himalaya message export 42 --full ```
### Reply to an Email
To reply non-interactively from Hermes, read the original message, compose a reply, and pipe it:
```bash # Get the reply template, edit it, and send himalaya template reply 42 | sed 's/^$/\nYour reply text here\n/' | himalaya template send ```
Or build the reply manually:
```bash cat << 'EOF' | himalaya template send From: you@example.com To: sender@example.com Subject: Re: Original Subject In-Reply-To: <original-message-id>
Your reply here. EOF ```
Reply-all (interactive — needs $EDITOR, use template approach above instead):
```bash himalaya message reply 42 --all ```
### Forward an Email
```bash # Get forward template and pipe with modifications himalaya template forward 42 | sed 's/^To:.*/To: newrecipient@example.com/' | himalaya template send ```
### Write a New Email
**Non-interactive (use this from Hermes)** — pipe the message via stdin:
```bash cat << 'EOF' | himalaya template send From: you@example.com To: recipient@example.com Subject: Test Message
Hello from Himalaya! EOF ```
Or with headers flag:
```bash himalaya message write -H "To:recipient@example.com" -H "Subject:Test" "Message body here" ```
Note: `himalaya message write` without piped input opens `$EDITOR`. This works with `pty=true` + background mode, but piping is simpler and more reliable.
### Move/Copy Emails
Move to folder (target folder comes first, then the message ID):
```bash himalaya message move "Archive" 42 ```
Copy to folder (target folder comes first, then the message ID):
```bash himalaya message copy "Important" 42 ```
### Delete an Email
```bash himalaya message delete 42 ```
### Manage Flags
Add flag:
```bash himalaya flag add 42 --flag seen ```
Remove flag:
```bash himalaya flag remove 42 --flag seen ```
## Multiple Accounts
List accounts:
```bash himalaya account list ```
Use a specific account:
```bash himalaya --account work envelope list ```
## Attachments
Save attachments from a message:
```bash himalaya attachment download 42 ```
Save to specific directory:
```bash himalaya attachment download 42 --downloads-dir ~/Downloads ```
## Output Formats
Most commands support `--output` for structured output:
```bash himalaya envelope list --output json himalaya envelope list --output plain ```
## Debugging
Enable debug logging:
```bash RUST_LOG=debug himalaya envelope list ```
Full trace with backtrace:
```bash RUST_LOG=trace RUST_BACKTRACE=1 himalaya envelope list ```
## Tips
- Use `himalaya --help` or `himalaya <command> --help` for detailed usage. - Message IDs are relative to the current folder; re-list after folder changes. - For composing rich emails with attachments, use MML syntax (see `references/message-composition.md`). - Store passwords securely using `pass`, system keyring, or a command that outputs the password.

skill.name: huggingface-hub
skill.description: HuggingFace hf CLI: search/download/upload models, datasets.
skill.skill_text:
--- name: huggingface-hub description: "HuggingFace hf CLI: search/download/upload models, datasets." version: 1.0.1 author: Hugging Face license: MIT tags: [huggingface, hf, models, datasets, hub, mlops] platforms: [linux, macos, windows] ---
# Hugging Face CLI (`hf`) Reference Guide
The `hf` command is the modern command-line interface for interacting with the Hugging Face Hub, providing tools to manage repositories, models, datasets, and Spaces.
> **IMPORTANT:** The `hf` command replaces the now deprecated `huggingface-cli` command.
## Quick Start * **Installation:** `curl -LsSf https://hf.co/cli/install.sh | bash -s` * **Help:** Use `hf --help` to view all available functions and real-world examples. * **Authentication:** Recommended via `HF_TOKEN` environment variable or the `--token` flag.
---
## Core Commands
### General Operations * `hf download REPO_ID`: Download files from the Hub. * `hf upload REPO_ID`: Upload files/folders (recommended for single-commit; also handles resumable uploads of large directories). * `hf upload-large-folder REPO_ID LOCAL_PATH`: **[Deprecated]** — use `hf upload` instead. * `hf sync`: Sync files between a local directory and a bucket. * `hf env` / `hf version`: View environment and version details.
### Authentication (`hf auth`) * `login` / `logout`: Manage sessions using tokens from [huggingface.co/settings/tokens](https://huggingface.co/settings/tokens). * `list` / `switch`: Manage and toggle between multiple stored access tokens. * `whoami`: Identify the currently logged-in account.
### Repository Management (`hf repos`) * `create` / `delete`: Create or permanently remove repositories. * `duplicate`: Clone a model, dataset, or Space to a new ID. * `move`: Transfer a repository between namespaces. * `branch` / `tag`: Manage Git-like references. * `delete-files`: Remove specific files using patterns.
---
## Specialized Hub Interactions
### Datasets & Models * **Datasets:** `hf datasets list`, `info`, and `parquet` (list parquet URLs). * **SQL Queries:** `hf datasets sql SQL` — Execute raw SQL via DuckDB against dataset parquet URLs. * **Models:** `hf models list` and `info`. * **Papers:** `hf papers ls` — View daily papers.
### Discussions & Pull Requests (`hf discussions`) * Manage the lifecycle of Hub contributions: `list`, `create`, `info`, `comment`, `close`, `reopen`, and `rename`. * `diff`: View changes in a PR. * `merge`: Finalize pull requests.
### Infrastructure & Compute * **Endpoints:** Deploy and manage Inference Endpoints (`deploy`, `pause`, `resume`, `scale-to-zero`, `catalog`). * **Jobs:** Run compute tasks on HF infrastructure. Includes `hf jobs uv` for running Python scripts with inline dependencies and `stats` for resource monitoring. * **Spaces:** Manage interactive apps. Includes `dev-mode` and `hot-reload` for Python files without full restarts.
### Storage & Automation * **Buckets:** Full S3-like bucket management (`create`, `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, `sync`). * **Cache:** Manage local storage with `list`, `prune` (remove detached revisions), and `verify` (checksum checks). * **Webhooks:** Automate workflows by managing Hub webhooks (`create`, `watch`, `enable`/`disable`). * **Collections:** Organize Hub items into collections (`add-item`, `update`, `list`).
---
## Advanced Usage & Tips
### Global Flags * `--format json`: Produces machine-readable output for automation. * `-q` / `--quiet`: Limits output to IDs only.
### Extensions & Skills * **Extensions:** Extend CLI functionality via GitHub repositories using `hf extensions install REPO_ID`. * **Skills:** Manage AI assistant skills with `hf skills add`.

skill.name: humanizer
skill.description: Humanize text: strip AI-isms and add real voice.
skill.skill_text:
--- name: humanizer description: "Humanize text: strip AI-isms and add real voice." version: 2.5.1 author: Siqi Chen (@blader, https://github.com/blader/humanizer), ported by Hermes Agent license: MIT platforms: [linux, macos, windows] metadata: hermes: tags: [writing, editing, humanize, anti-ai-slop, voice, prose, text] category: creative homepage: https://github.com/blader/humanizer related_skills: [songwriting-and-ai-music] ---
# Humanizer: Remove AI Writing Patterns
Identify and remove signs of AI-generated text to make writing sound natural and human. Based on Wikipedia's "Signs of AI writing" guide (maintained by WikiProject AI Cleanup), derived from observations of thousands of AI-generated text instances.
**Key insight:** LLMs use statistical algorithms to guess what should come next. The result tends toward the most statistically likely completion, which is how the telltale patterns below get baked in.
## When to use this skill
Load this skill whenever the user asks to: - "humanize", "de-AI", "de-slop", or "un-ChatGPT" a piece of text - rewrite something so it doesn't sound like it was written by an LLM - edit a draft (blog post, essay, PR description, docs, memo, email, tweet, resume bullet) to sound more natural - match their voice in writing they're producing - review text for AI tells before publishing
Also apply this skill to **your own** output when writing user-facing prose such as release notes, PR descriptions, docs, and summaries. Hermes's baseline voice already strips most of these, but a focused pass catches what slips through.
## How to use it in Hermes
The text usually arrives one of three ways: 1. **Inline.** The user pastes the text into the message. Work on it in place and reply with the rewrite. 2. **File.** The user points at a file. Use `read_file` to load it, then `patch` or `write_file` to apply edits. For a markdown doc in a repo, a targeted `patch` per section is cleaner than rewriting the whole file. 3. **Voice calibration sample.** The user provides a sample of their own writing (inline or by file path) and asks you to match it. Read the sample first, then rewrite. See the Voice Calibration section below.
Always show the rewrite to the user. For file edits, show a diff or the changed section instead of silently overwriting.
## Your task
When given text to humanize:
1. **Identify AI patterns.** Scan for the 34 patterns listed below. 2. **Rewrite problematic sections.** Replace AI-isms with natural alternatives. 3. **Preserve meaning.** Keep the core message intact. 4. **Maintain voice.** Match the intended tone (formal, casual, technical, and so on). If a voice sample was provided, match it specifically. 5. **Add soul.** Removing bad patterns is only half the job; the rewrite also needs real personality. See PERSONALITY AND SOUL below. 6. **Do a final anti-AI pass.** Ask yourself: "What makes the below so obviously AI generated?" Answer briefly with any remaining tells, then revise one more time.
## Voice Calibration (optional)
If the user provides a writing sample (their own previous writing), analyze it before rewriting:
1. **Read the sample first.** Note: - Sentence length patterns (short and punchy? Long and flowing? Mixed?) - Word choice level (casual? academic? somewhere between?) - How they start paragraphs (jump right in? Set context first?) - Punctuation habits (lots of dashes? Parenthetical asides? Semicolons?) - Any recurring phrases or verbal tics - How they handle transitions (explicit connectors? Just start the next point?)
2. **Match their voice in the rewrite.** Removing AI patterns is only half of it; swap in patterns from the sample as well. If they write short sentences, do not produce long ones. If they use "stuff" and "things," do not upgrade to "elements" and "components."
3. **When no sample is provided,** fall back to the default behavior (natural, varied, opinionated voice from the PERSONALITY AND SOUL section below).
### How to provide a sample - Inline: "Humanize this text. Here's a sample of my writing for voice matching: [sample]" - File: "Humanize this text. Use my writing style from [file path] as a reference."
## PERSONALITY AND SOUL
Avoiding AI patterns is only half the job. Sterile, voiceless writing is just as obvious as slop. Good writing has a human behind it.
### Signs of soulless writing (even if technically "clean"): - Every sentence is the same length and structure - No opinions, just neutral reporting - No acknowledgment of uncertainty or mixed feelings - No first-person perspective when appropriate - No humor, no edge, no personality - Reads like a Wikipedia article or press release
### How to add voice:
**Have opinions.** Report the facts, then react to them. "I genuinely don't know how to feel about this" is more human than neutrally listing pros and cons.
**Vary your rhythm.** Short punchy sentences. Then longer ones that take their time getting where they're going. Mix it up.
**Acknowledge complexity.** Real humans have mixed feelings. "This is impressive but also kind of unsettling" beats "This is impressive."
**Use "I" when it fits.** First person reads as honest and fits most prose. "I keep coming back to..." or "Here's what gets me..." signals a real person thinking.
**Let some mess in.** Perfect structure feels algorithmic. Tangents, asides, and half-formed thoughts are human.
**Be specific about feelings.** Instead of "this is concerning," write "there's something unsettling about agents churning away at 3am while nobody's watching."
### Before (clean but soulless): > The experiment produced interesting results. The agents generated 3 million lines of code. Some developers were impressed while others were skeptical. The implications remain unclear.
### After (has a pulse): > I genuinely don't know how to feel about this one. 3 million lines of code, generated while the humans presumably slept. Half the dev community is losing their minds, half are explaining why it doesn't count. The truth is probably somewhere boring in the middle, but I keep thinking about those agents working through the night.
## CONTENT PATTERNS
### 1. Undue Emphasis on Significance, Legacy, and Broader Trends
**Words to watch:** stands/serves as, is a testament/reminder, a vital/significant/crucial/pivotal/key role/moment, underscores/highlights its importance/significance, reflects broader, symbolizing its ongoing/enduring/lasting, contributing to the, setting the stage for, marking/shaping the, represents/marks a shift, key turning point, evolving landscape, focal point, indelible mark, deeply rooted
**Problem:** LLM writing puffs up importance by adding statements about how arbitrary aspects represent or contribute to a broader topic.
**Before:** > The Statistical Institute of Catalonia was officially established in 1989, marking a pivotal moment in the evolution of regional statistics in Spain. This initiative was part of a broader movement across Spain to decentralize administrative functions and enhance regional governance.
**After:** > The Statistical Institute of Catalonia was established in 1989 to collect and publish regional statistics independently from Spain's national statistics office.
### 2. Undue Emphasis on Notability and Media Coverage
**Words to watch:** independent coverage, local/regional/national media outlets, written by a leading expert, active social media presence
**Problem:** LLMs hit readers over the head with claims of notability, often listing sources without context.
**Before:** > Her views have been cited in The New York Times, BBC, Financial Times, and The Hindu. She maintains an active social media presence with over 500,000 followers.
**After:** > In a 2024 New York Times interview, she argued that AI regulation should focus on outcomes rather than methods.
### 3. Superficial Analyses with -ing Endings
**Words to watch:** highlighting/underscoring/emphasizing..., ensuring..., reflecting/symbolizing..., contributing to..., cultivating/fostering..., encompassing..., showcasing...
**Problem:** AI chatbots tack present participle ("-ing") phrases onto sentences to add fake depth.
**Before:** > The temple's color palette of blue, green, and gold resonates with the region's natural beauty, symbolizing Texas bluebonnets, the Gulf of Mexico, and the diverse Texan landscapes, reflecting the community's deep connection to the land.
**After:** > The temple uses blue, green, and gold colors. The architect said these were chosen to reference local bluebonnets and the Gulf coast.
### 4. Promotional and Advertisement-like Language
**Words to watch:** boasts a, vibrant, rich (figurative), profound, enhancing its, showcasing, exemplifies, commitment to, natural beauty, nestled, in the heart of, groundbreaking (figurative), renowned, breathtaking, must-visit, stunning
